item.title: The Meaning and Facets of `Symmetry' in Physics
item.description: arXiv:2610.12488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is an English translation of a contribution to the latest German edition (2017) of Hermann Weyl's classic text "Symmetry", edited and annotated by Erhard Scholz, Klaus Volkert, and myself. In this contribution I discuss various physical aspects of the notion of symmetry and place them in context from the perspective of theoretical physics. In particular, a distinction is drawn between symmetries of individual configurations (solutions of equilibrium equations or equations of motion) and symmetries of the laws themselves. Likewise, a distinction is made between those operations that alter physical states and so-called gauge symmetries, which leave physical states unchanged and merely represent a redundancy in the mathematical description. Besides gauge symmetries, I comment on the connection to conservation laws, symmetry breaking, and the philosophy of space.
item.dc:creator: Domenico Giulini

item.title: On the Utility of Textbooks in Understanding the Renaissance of General Relativity
item.description: arXiv:2610.13562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper argues for the historical utility of general relativity textbooks written during, or shortly before, the Renaissance of general relativity. More so than research papers, textbooks offer a narrative account of the field--one that may differ substantially from the accounts of other authors addressing the same subject. Textbooks on general relativity therefore constitute a distinctive form of testimony to the intellectual forces that shaped general relativity, particularly during its reinvention period from 1955 to the mid-1970s. A second pillar of this argument is the observation that nearly all principal investigators at the research centers previously identified by Lalli et al.--centers that functioned as intellectual epicenters of the Renaissance of general relativity--eventually produced a textbook associated with their own school of thought. To situate this observation within the broader development of the field, the paper presents a concise history of general relativity textbooks from the theory's inception in 1915-16 to the 1980s. This history illustrates one way in which textbooks can serve as sources for reconstructing the intellectual dynamics of the Renaissance of general relativity.
item.dc:creator: Bernadette Lessel

item.title: A Review on the Properties and Nature of Light
item.description: arXiv:2610.13932v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The following paper is a detailed review on the properties and nature in relation to the phenomena known as 'light'. The paper tries to chronologically detail the development of theories and related experiments from the philosophical Greco-Roman and Indian schools of thought to the modern quantum theories.
item.dc:creator: Prachurjo Dutta Roy

item.title: Determinism and Indeterminism as Model Artefacts: Toward a Model-Invariant Ontology of Physics
item.description: arXiv:2512.22540v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper argues that, where deterministic and indeterministic formulations agree on empirically corroborated structure while differing in their completion of structure that remains empirically underdetermined, features invariant across these formulations warrant ontological commitment, whereas any warrant attaching to features that vary across them is categorically more provisional. Because deterministic and indeterministic completions are always formally available, while additional grounds for preferring particular completions are contingent and defeasible, empirically corroborated structure alone cannot determine whether reality is fundamentally deterministic or indeterministic, or whether that very distinction belongs only to specific representations of it. On this basis, I advance a model-invariance criterion according to which structural features are candidates for realist commitment insofar as they are empirically corroborated within a regime and preserved across the admissible formulations of that structure. I show how such invariant content can be characterised in mathematically intelligible ways, yielding a fallibilist form of structural realism grounded in model-invariance rather than in the specific form of any given mathematical representation. Features such as conservation relations, invariant measures, symmetries, and probability or correlation structures over observable histories may satisfy this criterion. By contrast, the localisation of modal selection---whether in fine-grained initial conditions, stochastic outcomes, or state-update and collapse mechanisms---may vary across empirically admissible formulations and therefore constitute a gauge-like representational freedom. This framework offers a realist ontology for modern physics that combines empirical openness with resistance to metaphysical overreach.
item.dc:creator: David Nolland
